summary.text: An iceberg is a piece of freshwater ice more than 15 meters long that has broken off a glacier or ice shelf and floats freely in open water.
Typically only about a tenth of its volume shows above water, since ice is less dense than seawater, and the shape of the hidden part is hard to judge from above.
Icebergs are a serious danger to ships, and as they melt and break apart they can flip over at any time without warning.

facts.label: Trapped air
facts.value: Up to 10% air bubbles by volume

items.prompt: A sailor sees an iceberg rising 10 m above the sea. Roughly how much of its volume is out of sight below the water?

options.label: About half
About a quarter
About nine-tenths
Almost none

items.explain: Typically about one-tenth of an iceberg's volume is above water, so about nine-tenths is hidden.

items.prompt: Why does an iceberg float in the ocean instead of sinking?

options.label: Its flat base spreads its weight like a raft
Ice is less dense than seawater
Ocean currents hold it up from below
Salt inside the ice makes it lighter

items.explain: By Archimedes's principle, pure ice at about 920 kg/m³ floats in seawater at about 1,025 kg/m³.

items.prompt: Kayakers drifting beside a melting iceberg hear a steady fizzing and popping. What makes the sound?

options.label: Squeezed air bubbles bursting from the ice
Salt crystals dissolving into the sea
Small fish feeding along the ice
The ice cracking as it gets colder

items.explain: Compressed air trapped in the ice is released as the melting surface reaches it, a sound nicknamed "Bergie Seltzer".

items.prompt: An iceberg has melted and broken unevenly on one side. Why might it suddenly roll over?

options.label: A gust of wind tips it past balance
The rising tide lifts one end of it
Seawater freezes onto its top and adds weight
Its center of gravity has shifted

items.explain: As an iceberg melts and breaks apart its center of gravity changes, which can make it capsize.

items.prompt: A few icebergs look dirty black instead of white. What causes that dark color?

options.label: Oil spilled from passing ships
Soot settling from the air
Sediment carried in the ice
A thick layer of dead algae

items.explain: Sediment can give some icebergs a dirty black coloration.

items.prompt: An iceberg has steep sides and a broad flat top, like a floating plateau. Where did it most likely come from?

options.label: An Antarctic ice shelf
A Greenland glacier
Frozen sea surface ice
A frozen river mouth

items.explain: Antarctic ice shelves often produce large flat-topped tabular icebergs, while Greenland glaciers often release irregular ones.

paragraphs.heading: A floating mountain of ice
paragraphs.text: An iceberg is a chunk of freshwater ice, more than 15 meters long, that has broken away from a glacier or an ice shelf and now floats freely in open water. Smaller floating pieces of glacier ice get their own names. Pieces less than 5 meters above the sea are called bergy bits, and those less than 1 meter high are called growlers. The word comes partly from the Dutch ijsberg, which means ice mountain.

paragraphs.heading: Mostly out of sight
paragraphs.text: Most of an iceberg sits underwater, and usually only about one-tenth of its volume shows. This follows from Archimedes's principle of buoyancy: pure ice has a density of about 920 kg/m³, a little less than seawater at about 1,025 kg/m³. The shape of the hidden part is hard to judge from what shows above the surface. Icebergs are treated as a serious hazard at sea. The same picture gave us the phrase tip of the iceberg, for a small visible part of a bigger hidden problem.

paragraphs.heading: Sizes and shapes
paragraphs.text: Icebergs come in many sizes and shapes. Those that break off Greenland's glaciers are often irregular, while Antarctic ice shelves tend to release large tabular, or table-top, icebergs. The largest icebergs on record broke off Antarctica's Ross Ice Shelf. A tabular berg sighted in 1956 measured 335 by 97 kilometres, bigger than Belgium, and the one named B-15 measured nearly 300 by 40 kilometres in 2000. Icebergs can rise more than 100 metres above the sea and weigh from about 100,000 tonnes to over 10 million tonnes.

paragraphs.heading: Drifting and wasting away
paragraphs.text: Once afloat, an iceberg breaks down by melting and fracturing. These change its mass, surface area, volume and stability, so the way it breaks down and the way it drifts are tied together. Sunlight and the heat and salt carried by the ocean melt it, and waves striking it help pieces break off. Winds and currents can push icebergs toward coasts, where they may freeze into pack ice. In shallow water they can touch the sea floor, which is called seabed gouging.

paragraphs.heading: Fizzing and flipping
paragraphs.text: Icebergs carry air from the snow that made them. As snow is squeezed into firn and then into glacier ice, air gets trapped as bubbles, and up to 10% of an iceberg's volume can be bubbles. When melting reaches them they burst with a fizzing, popping sound that some call Bergie Seltzer. Icebergs can also flip over as they melt and break apart, since their center of gravity shifts. This can happen soon after a berg breaks off, or at any time with no warning.

paragraphs.heading: Colors and glacial earthquakes
paragraphs.text: Most icebergs look white because snow covers them. Yet some are green, blue, yellow or black, some are striped, and a few show rainbow colors. Seawater, algae and ice without air bubbles produce many of these colors, and sediment can give a berg a dirty black look. Large icebergs can even cause earthquakes. When one breaks off a glacier front and flips onto the glacier face, it can push the whole glacier backward for a moment and release as much energy as an atomic bomb.
